title: Handle the collection and storage of the table eggs on the farm

lessons.title: Collecting table eggs
lessons.html:
Table eggs and why care matters

Table eggs are eggs laid by commercial layer hens for people to eat. They are not fertile. Every egg is food, so it must be handled cleanly and gently. A cracked or dirty egg can carry germs such as Salmonella, and it loses money for the farm because it is sold at a lower price or thrown away.

Before collection

  • Wear clean overalls and, where required, a hairnet.
  • Wash and sanitise your hands.
  • Use clean, undamaged trays. Dirty or broken trays crack and dirty the eggs.
  • Check that the collection trolley is clean and its wheels move smoothly.

How often to collect

Collect eggs at the times on your farm's schedule – usually more than once a day, with most eggs laid in the morning. Collecting often means eggs spend less time where hens can peck, step on or dirty them, and they get to the cool store sooner.

Collecting from cages and conveyor belts

In cage and many barn systems, eggs roll onto a belt that carries them to the end of the house or to a packing area. Your tasks:

  • Run the belts at the set times and watch for eggs bumping and piling up; stop the belt if eggs crash into each other.
  • Pick up eggs stuck in the cage front or roll-out area by hand.
  • Keep belts and egg-saver wires clean and report broken parts.

Collecting by hand from nests and floors

In free-range and barn houses, collect from nest boxes and look for floor eggs in corners and under slats. Keep floor eggs separate – they are dirtier.

Handling each egg

  1. Pick up eggs gently with your fingers, not by grabbing many at once.
  2. Place each egg in the tray pointed end down. This keeps the air cell at the top and the yolk centred, which keeps the egg fresher.
  3. Do not overfill trays or stack them too high on the trolley.
  4. Push trolleys slowly; avoid bumps and sudden stops.

Count eggs as you collect, or record the belt counter, and write the total on the house record.

lessons.title: Sorting eggs on the farm
lessons.html:
First sorting

Before eggs go to the packhouse or into storage, they are checked and sorted. The farm's grading rules and the regulations for eggs under the Agricultural Product Standards Act set out the grades and sizes. Your supervisor will show you the farm's standard. On the farm, the main job is to remove eggs that are not fit to go with good eggs.

Eggs to remove

TypeWhat to do
Cracked or broken eggsRemove; broken eggs go in a closed bin. Cracked eggs are handled as the farm decides.
Dirty eggs (manure, blood, yolk on the shell)Separate tray. Do not wipe with a wet dirty cloth.
Floor eggsSeparate tray, clearly marked.
Misshapen, very thin-shelled or soft-shelled eggsSeparate tray as rejects.

Cleaning dirty eggs

An eggshell has tiny holes (pores) and a natural protective coating. Rough cleaning removes the coating and can push germs inside. Only clean eggs using the method your farm allows, for example dry cleaning with a clean abrasive pad or a proper egg-washing machine with the correct water temperature and sanitiser. Never soak eggs in a bucket of water.

Checking size and shell quality

Eggs are sold in sizes such as small, medium, large, extra large and jumbo, based on mass. On many farms the packhouse grading machine weighs them. When you sort by hand, use the farm scale and chart. Notice and report changes: many thin shells, pale shells, small eggs or blood spots can mean a problem with the flock's feed, health or age.

Why report?

A sudden rise in cracked or dirty eggs tells the manager something: rough trolley handling, a broken belt, too few collections, dirty nests or sick hens. Your counts help fix the cause.

lessons.title: Storing eggs and keeping records
lessons.html:
The egg store

Once collected and sorted, eggs must go to the egg store quickly. Freshness drops fast in a warm house or passage.

Good storage conditions

  • Cool and steady – keep the store at the temperature your farm procedure states, and check the thermometer every day. Record the reading.
  • Avoid "sweating" – if cold eggs are taken out into warm, humid air, water drops form on the shell. This wet shell lets germs in. Keep temperatures steady and follow the farm's rules for moving eggs out of the cool store.
  • Clean and dry – sweep and clean the floor and shelves. No broken eggs or yolk left lying.
  • No strong smells – eggs take up smells. Never store eggs near diesel, paraffin, chemicals, onions, fish or disinfectants.
  • Pests out – keep doors closed and screens in place against flies, rats and birds.

Stacking and labelling

  • Stack trays straight and not higher than the farm limit, on pallets off the floor.
  • Leave space around stacks for cold air to move.
  • Label each stack or pallet with the house number, date laid and grade or type (for example "floor" or "dirty").

First in, first out

Older eggs must leave first. This is called FIFO – first in, first out. Put new eggs behind or to one side of older eggs, so older eggs are dispatched first. Never mix dates in one stack.

Records

Write down on the egg record every day:

  • Number of eggs collected per house and per collection.
  • Number of cracked, dirty, floor and reject eggs.
  • Egg store temperature.
  • Eggs dispatched, date and to whom.

Records let the farm trace eggs back to a house and date if a customer complains or a food safety problem is found. Write neatly, honestly and on time.

Key points

  • Collect eggs often and gently, with clean hands and clean trays, pointed end down.
  • Remove cracked, dirty, floor and misshapen eggs and keep them separate.
  • Never soak eggs in water; clean only by the method the farm allows.
  • Store eggs cool and steady, away from strong smells, and avoid sweating.
  • Use first in, first out, label stacks, and keep accurate daily egg records.

It stops the egg from being fertile

Fresh eggs in front, old eggs out
